analysis.one_liner: Repeals Medicare's new catastrophic coverage and its income-based premium before most benefits begin.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed this repeal 99-0 just two days after it was introduced, but the House never voted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: In 1988 Congress created Medicare catastrophic coverage, including a cap on out-of-pocket costs and new prescription drug help, paid for partly by a premium that rose with a beneficiary's income. This bill undoes those provisions before they took effect, keeps a restructured nursing-home benefit of 100 days after a hospital stay, and requires insurers to offer to restore Medigap policies that seniors had dropped. It swept the Senate within three days of introduction but never received a House vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, especially those with higher incomes, are spared the new premiums that financed catastrophic coverage. Seniors who dropped private Medigap policies after the 1988 law passed get a limited window to have them restored on their pre-1989 terms. Sponsors also preserved a slimmed-down extended-care benefit: 100 days of post-hospital nursing care per year, with modified coinsurance.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the supplemental Medicare premium imposed on beneficiaries whose tax liability equaled or exceeded $150, and repeals the catastrophic-coverage provisions that premium financed, retroactive to the 1988 law.

Requires insurers that sold Medicare supplemental policies to people who terminated coverage as of January 1, 1989 to offer continuation of that coverage on terms at least as favorable as those in effect on December 31, 1988, including treatment of pre-existing conditions and group rating.
Preserves coverage of post-hospital extended care for up to 100 days per calendar year, with coinsurance set at one-eighth of the hospital deductible per day after the first 20 days.

analysis.who_pays: Medicare beneficiaries lose the protections the 1988 law would have provided: the cap on out-of-pocket Part B costs, outpatient prescription drug coverage, respite care for chronically dependent people, and screening mammography (delayed a year). Seniors without private supplemental coverage face unlimited out-of-pocket exposure and pay for their own prescriptions.

drawbacks.text: Repeals the cap on individual out-of-pocket expenses under Medicare Part B and the new prescription drug coverage, leaving beneficiaries to bear catastrophic costs themselves.
Cuts Medicare extended care coverage from 150 days per calendar year to 100 and reinstates the requirement that the care follow a qualifying hospital stay.

Delays the home intravenous drug therapy and screening mammography programs by one year and delays in-home respite care for chronically dependent individuals from 1990 to 1991, while tightening its eligibility criteria.

The repeal removes the financing mechanism that would have made the new protections available to all beneficiaries, including low-income seniors, not just those who could buy private supplemental coverage.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's real benefit was relieving beneficiaries of a new, widely resented premium that rose with income, and its Medigap-restoration provision gave real protection to seniors who had dropped private policies expecting public coverage to replace them. But the cost is substantial: the 1988 law's out-of-pocket cap and drug benefit were precisely the protections that mattered most to sicker, poorer seniors, and the income-based premium was the only reason those protections could be offered to everyone. The repeal solved a financing-design grievance by eliminating the benefit itself.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed it 99-0 within three days of introduction, but the bill sat at the House desk for the rest of the Congress and never got a House vote.

narrative.text: Sen. John McCain introduced the bill on October 4, 1989, with 32 cosponsors (31 Republicans and 1 Democrat).
The bill was laid before the Senate by unanimous consent on October 6, and the sponsor modified it before floor action, bypassing committee consideration.
On October 6, the Senate agreed 96-3 to waive the Budget Act for the bill; the 3 no votes were Democrats, and all 45 Republicans voted yes.

A motion to commit the bill to the Senate Finance Committee, which would have sent it through regular committee review, was rejected 12-87; the 12 yes votes were all Democrats, and all 45 Republicans voted no.
The Senate passed the bill as modified, 99-0, with 54 of 55 Democrats and 45 of 45 Republicans voting yes.
The bill was then held at the desk and no House action followed; the Congress ended January 3, 1991 without a House vote on this version.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Beneficiaries facing the largest premium increases were spared them, and the private Medicare supplemental insurance market kept its role as the channel for coverage Medicare itself did not provide. Seniors who would have received the new drug and out-of-pocket protections, particularly those without private coverage, came out with nothing.

sides.party_line_note: Final passage was 99-0 (54-0 among Democrats, 45-0 among Republicans); the only visible dissent was 3 Democrats on a budget-waiver vote and 12 Democrats voting to slow the bill down in committee.

industries.note: Repealing public catastrophic coverage preserves private Medigap policies as the only way beneficiaries can fill Medicare's gaps, protecting the industry's customer base. The bill does impose one obligation: insurers must offer a limited-window continuation, on pre-1989 terms, to policyholders who dropped coverage expecting the public benefit to take over.
The bill cuts Medicare-paid extended care from 150 days per year to 100 and restricts coverage to care following a hospital stay, shrinking a benefit the facilities would have billed against.
Repeal eliminates Medicare's new outpatient drug coverage, leaving only immunosuppressants and home IV drugs covered, so the industry forgoes a new public payer for seniors' prescriptions.
HMOs contracting with Medicare are required to adjust their agreements with beneficiaries to reflect the repeal, a compliance burden with no offsetting gain in this bill.
